claims.text: The Galveston County Consolidated Drainage District installed seven flood sensors in Friendswood and League City as part of a new flood warning system now online.
claims.quote: The Galveston County Consolidated Drainage District has installed seven flood sensors in Friendswood and League City, part of a new system officials say could help residents track rising water levels in real time and better prepare for dangerous flooding conditions.

claims.text: The sensors come from Simplicity Integration and run on Axonis Decision Intelligence.
claims.quote: The sensors are provided by Simplicity Integration and powered by Axonis Decision Intelligence, a technology company focused on water and flood intelligence.

claims.text: Six sensors are in the Clear Creek watershed and one is in the Dickinson Bayou watershed.
claims.quote: District leaders say six sensors are located in the Clear Creek watershed and one is in the Dickinson Bayou watershed.

claims.text: According to the company, the system combines real-time sensor data with public rainfall totals, stream gauge readings, weather station data and soil saturation conditions.
claims.quote: According to the company, the system combines real-time sensor data with public information including rainfall totals, stream gauge readings, weather station data and soil saturation conditions.

claims.text: The public map uses colours: green for safe, yellow for flooding possible, red for flooding likely.
claims.quote: Officials say the map uses color-coded indicators to show flood conditions: Green indicates safe conditions Yellow indicates flooding possible Red indicates flooding likely

claims.text: Jason Jones, secretary of the drainage district board, said Galveston County had no flood sensors at all before this.
claims.quote: “With no flood sensors at all in Galveston County, this was a very obvious step in the right direction,” said Jason Jones, secretary of the Galveston County Consolidated Drainage District board.

claims.text: Alison Reese, COO and co-founder of Simplicity Integration, said lead time lets people get out of the way in plenty of time.
claims.quote: “If they can give that level of warning and that amount of lead time, then people can get themselves — and whatever people love that are in their houses — out of the way in plenty of time,” Reese said.

claims.text: Jones said people in low areas or in cars need to check passable routes out of town.
claims.quote: “For a person like me with a big truck, I’m worried about how can I get home,” Jones said. “But if you live in one of the lower areas, or if you’re in a car, you need to look to see your passable routes out of town. So that’s very crucial.”

claims.text: Each sensor cost less than $10,000, the sensors were deployed at seven sites, and they went live in April.
claims.quote: The sensors — which each cost less than $10,000 — were deployed at seven sites and went live in April.

claims.text: The district deployed a network of radar sensors to monitor water levels.
claims.quote: The district, which is located about 30 miles south of Houston, recently deployed a network of radar sensors as part of a broader flood data intelligence platform that officials will use to monitor water levels across the cities of Friendswood and League.

claims.text: The platform sends automated localized text alerts when sensors detect water rising to an at-risk level set by officials.
claims.quote: The platform will also send automated, localized text alerts to people if the sensor system detects that water is rising to an at-risk level determined by officials, said Alison Reese, Simplicity Integration’s chief operating officer and co-founder.

claims.text: Jones said neighborhoods still remember Hurricane Harvey and Tropical Storm Allison, people look at the creek every day, and now they can check from their phone.
claims.quote: Jones said the technology is especially meaningful in neighborhoods that still remember devastating floods from storms like Hurricane Harvey and Tropical Storm Allison. “People come outside and look at the creek every day. It’s almost like PTSD from Harvey and other rain events,” Jones said. “Now from their phone, they can be in their home or they could be anywhere in the world and access this data in real time.”

claims.text: The platform uses AI tools to analyze the data and help predict how flood conditions could develop.
claims.quote: The platform then uses artificial intelligence tools to analyze the information and help predict how flood conditions could develop.

claims.text: The technology can analyze how upstream conditions could affect neighborhoods farther downstream.
claims.quote: The technology can also analyze how conditions upstream could affect neighborhoods farther downstream.

claims.text: Jones said the system could help residents decide whether roads are passable or whether it is time to evacuate.
claims.quote: Jones said the system could help residents make critical decisions during severe weather — including whether roads are still passable or whether it may be time to evacuate.

claims.text: Residents can watch sensor locations on a public web portal and sign up for alerts tied to specific creeks or monitoring points.
claims.quote: The system also includes a public web portal where residents can monitor sensor locations in real time and sign up for alerts tied to specific creeks or monitoring points.

claims.text: For now the sensors are online only in Friendswood and League City, and officials hope to expand to other parts of Galveston County.
claims.quote: Right now, the sensors are only online in Friendswood and League City, but officials say they hope to eventually expand the technology into other parts of Galveston County.

claims.text: Board president Rusty Burkett called flooding and drainage the number one threat to lives and property in Galveston County.
claims.quote: “I think flooding and drainage [are] the number one threat to lives and property in Galveston County,” Burkett said.

claims.text: Burkett said the district will get accurate predictive flooding information, which has never happened before.
claims.quote: “We're going to get some really accurate information about predictive flooding, which has never happened before.”

claims.text: The district covers more than 20 square miles of northern Galveston County and maintains more than 80 miles of creeks, ditches and bayous.
claims.quote: Galveston County Consolidated Drainage District's jurisdiction encompasses more than 20 square miles of northern Galveston County. The District maintains more than 80 miles of creeks, ditches, and bayous, as well as subdivision detention ponds and other joint projects and works closely with the City of Friendswood

claims.text: The district plans to add LiDAR sensors that monitor water flow.
claims.quote: GCCDD is planning to expand its sensor network to include LiDAR sensors that will monitor the flow of water for enhanced insights, which Burkett said will be critical for predicting flooding conditions and events in communities.

claims.text: Executive director Paige Bailey said the system has already mapped places that need more stream gauges and sensors.
claims.quote: The flood intelligence system has “already mapped out some locations where we need more stream gauges, more sensors and some additional LiDAR [sensors] … in order to give our community the best possible information,” Bailey said.

claims.text: The system can connect to existing infrastructure to trigger sirens or activate barrier systems.
claims.quote: The system can also connect with existing infrastructure to, for instance, trigger sirens or activate barrier systems that look to manage incoming flood waters.

claims.text: Galveston County is the first live production instance of the SI-Ai platform, which went live in April 2026.
claims.quote: Axonis and Simplicity Integration have deployed an AI-powered flood warning system in Galveston County, Texas, marking the first live production instance of their jointly developed SI-Ai platform. The system went live in April 2026

claims.text: Rusty Burkett is the drainage district's board president.
claims.quote: said Rusty Burkett, the district’s board president.

claims.text: Paige Bailey is executive director and general counsel of the drainage district.
claims.quote: said Paige Bailey, executive director and general counsel of GCCDD.
